claims.evidence: This describes the physical arrangement of the MCAM system, shown in Appendix 1—figure 1.

claims.claim: Each CMOS sensor contains 10 megapixels (4320x2432) and a pixel size of 1.4 µm for a 6 mm x 3.4 mm active area.
claims.source: Each CMOS sensor (Omnivision, OV10823) contains 10 megapixels (4320x2432) and a pixel size of 1.4 µm for a 6 mm x 3.4 mm active area.
claims.evidence: This provides technical specifications of the CMOS sensors used in the MCAM.

claims.claim: The sensors were placed at a 19 mm pitch.
claims.source: The sensors were placed at a 19 mm pitch, and their rectangular active area allows us to capture overlapping field-of-view information primarily along one dimension for stereo-based depth tracking and dual-channel fluorescence imaging.
claims.evidence: This describes the physical spacing of sensors in the MCAM.

claims.claim: The imaging system's total number of recorded pixels per frame is 0.96 gigapixels.
claims.source: The imaging system's total number of recorded pixels per frame is 0.96 gigapixels.
claims.evidence: This is a direct measurement of the MCAM's pixel count.

claims.claim: The MCAM can operate in a 'full-frame' mode that records video data from all 96 micro-cameras at an aggregate frame rate of approximately 1 frame per second.
claims.source: The MCAM offers two modes of operation. First, it can operate in a 'full-frame' mode that records video data from all 96 micro-cameras at an aggregate frame rate of approximately 1 frame per second (see timing diagram in Appendix 1—figure 4B–C).
claims.evidence: This describes one operational mode of the MCAM system.

claims.claim: The per-frame exposure time for each individual camera can be reduced to approximately 1ms to limit any per-frame motion blur.
claims.source: The per-frame exposure time for each individual camera can be reduced to approximately 1ms to limit any per-frame motion blur.
claims.evidence: This describes a technical capability of the MCAM system.

claims.claim: The MCAM architecture offers the flexibility to read data from a smaller number of sensors at a higher frame rate.
claims.source: The MCAM architecture also offers the flexibility to read data from a smaller number of sensors at a higher frame rate.
claims.evidence: This describes an alternative operational mode of the MCAM system.

claims.claim: A 'single-sensor' mode of operation allows selective recording of video data from up to four electronically assigned micro-cameras at a frame rate of approximately 12 frames per second.
claims.source: For example, a 'single-sensor' mode of operation allows us to selectively record video data from up to four electronically assigned micro-cameras at a frame rate of approximately 12 frames per second (Appendix 1—figure 5).
claims.evidence: This describes another operational mode of the MCAM system.

claims.claim: Each of the 96 cameras utilizes a multi-element 12 mm diameter mount lens with 25 mm focal length and 2.5 f-number.
claims.source: Each of the 96 cameras utilizes a multi-element 12 mm diameter mount lens (Edmund Optics 58–207, 25 mm focal length, 2.5 f-number), with an 18 mm maximum outer diameter that currently sets the MCAM's inter-camera spacing (to 19 mm).
claims.evidence: This provides technical specifications of the lenses used in the MCAM.

claims.claim: The MCAM lenses offer approximately 18 µm full-pitch resolution at a 150 mm working distance that extends across the entire per-sensor image FOV.
claims.source: As shown in Appendix 1—figure 2, these lenses offer approximately 18 µm full-pitch resolution at a 150 mm working distance that extends across the entire per-sensor image FOV with the employed 10 Megapixel rectangular image sensors (1.4 µm pixels, 3.4 mm x 6 mm).
claims.evidence: This is a measurement of the optical resolution of the MCAM system, shown in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claims.claim: The system's theoretical Rayleigh criterion for axial resolution under incoherent imaging conditions is DRay = 0.28 mm.
claims.source: First, we use the system's theoretical Rayleigh criterion for axial resolution under incoherent imaging conditions to estimate DRay = 0.28 mm.
claims.evidence: This is a calculated theoretical value for the MCAM's axial resolution.

claims.claim: The axial sample range across which lateral resolution remains within a factor of 2 of its maximum value at the plane of best focus is DRes = 2.54 mm.
claims.source: Second, we experimentally measured the axial sample range across which lateral resolution remains within a factor of 2 of its maximum value at the plane of best focus as DRes = 2.54 mm, which we found to be a useful measure of practical axial imaging extent.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental measurement of the MCAM's depth of field.

claims.claim: The full-width half-maximum of image contrast as a function of axial distance from the plane of best focus is DCon = 1.95 mm.
claims.source: Third, we experimentally measured the full-width half-maximum of image contrast (defined as the average mean image gradient magnitude of a resolution target) as a function of axial distance from the plane of best focus as DCon = 1.95 mm.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental measurement of the MCAM's depth of field based on image contrast.

claims.claim: The current MCAM design offers approximately 52% image overlap along the longer sensor dimension and <10% overlap along the shorter image dimension.
claims.source: By using rectangular image sensors with a height/width ratio of 1/1.8, the current MCAM design offers approximately 52% image overlap along the longer sensor dimension and <10% overlap along the shorter image dimension.
claims.evidence: This describes the overlapping field-of-view configuration of the MCAM.

claims.claim: The overlapping field-of-view configuration guarantees that any point within the object plane (neglecting edge regions) is imaged by at least two micro-cameras.
claims.source: This overlapping field-of-view configuration is diagrammed in Appendix 1—figures 2 and 4 and guarantees that any point within the object plane (neglecting edge regions) is imaged by at least two micro-cameras.
claims.evidence: This is a consequence of the MCAM's design, shown in Appendix 1—figures 2 and 4.

claims.claim: Packaged 10 MP CMOS sensors were $30 apiece in quantities of 100.
claims.source: Packaged 10 MP CMOS sensors (Omnivision OV10823) were $30 apiece in quantities of 100.
claims.evidence: This is a factual statement about component costs for the MCAM.

claims.claim: Imaging lenses were $75 apiece in quantities of 100.
claims.source: Imaging lenses were $75 apiece in quantities of 100.
claims.evidence: This is a factual statement about component costs for the MCAM.

claims.claim: FPGAs were $267 apiece for 16 units.
claims.source: FPGAs were $267 apiece for 16 units.
claims.evidence: This is a factual statement about component costs for the MCAM.

claims.claim: For the presented MCAM with 96 imagers, the total price of key components is $14,352.
claims.source: For the presented MCAM with 96 imagers, the total price of these key components is $14,352.
claims.evidence: This is a calculated total cost based on the component prices listed.

claims.claim: A continuous recording session at 0.74 Hz lasted almost one hour and resulted in 2.5 TB of unstitched data (2649 frames, 962 MB per frame) and 1.17 TB stitched data (442 MB per image).
claims.source: A continuous recording session at 0.74 Hz lasted almost one hour resulted in 2.5 TB of unstitched data (2649 frames, 962 MB per frame) and 1.17 TB stitched data (442 MB per image).
claims.evidence: This is a measurement of data volume from an actual MCAM recording session.

claims.claim: The system exploits the rapid current read/write speeds for individual solid state drives on a single personal computer (achieving approx. 1 GB/s).
claims.source: The system exploits the rapid current read/write speeds for individual solid state drives on a single personal computer (achieving approx. 1 GB/s), and marks a significant speedup from previously published gigapixel imaging systems (Brady et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is a measurement of the MCAM's data transfer speed and comparison to prior work.

claims.claim: In an MCAM image, a zebrafish (8 dpf) is captured by 9699±2758 pixels (n=93 zebrafish).
claims.source: In an MCAM image, a zebrafish (8 dpf) is captured by 9699±2758 pixels (n=93 zebrafish), which is significantly higher than in standard imaging systems.
claims.evidence: This is a measurement of pixel count per zebrafish in MCAM images.

claims.claim: When using a single 20 MP camera with the same large-FOV, fish would be represented by less than 400 pixels.
claims.source: For example, when using a single 20 MP camera with the same large-FOV, fish would be represented by less than 400 pixels, and even less in older juvenile fish (Romero-Ferrero et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison calculation showing the advantage of MCAM over standard cameras.

claims.claim: For a standard 3 MP camera sensor imaging a comparable FOV, a fish occupies less than ~100 pixels.
claims.source: For a standard 3 MP camera sensor imaging a comparable FOV, a fish occupies less than ~100 pixels (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison calculation shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Stereoscopic depth measurement using the MCAM yields approximately 100 µm accuracy in depth localization over a >5 mm depth range.
claims.source: Using this stereoscopic depth measurement approach yields approximately 100 µm accuracy in depth localization over a>5 mm depth range (see Appendix 1—figure 7 and associated Appendix 1 for experimental support).
claims.evidence: This is a measurement of the MCAM's depth tracking accuracy, with experimental support in Appendix 1—figure 7.

claims.claim: Videos captured approximately 58,000 worms per frame in C. elegans experiments.
claims.source: Videos captured ~58,000 worms per frame, captured at about 450 pixels per worm within a typical gigapixel video (averaged across 20 frames, single frame in Figure 3A–C, top).
claims.evidence: This is a measurement of organism count and pixel resolution in C. elegans experiments.

claims.claim: The NYL2629 C. elegans strain shows previously unreported swarming behavior.
claims.source: Surprisingly, both the unc-3 mutants, and especially the NYL2629 strain show previously unreported swarming behavior.
claims.evidence: This is a novel observation made using the MCAM system.

claims.claim: Approximately 3 days after being transferred to a new nutrient lawn, the NYL2629 strain began to form tight swarms that tiled most of the petri dish in a semi-periodic fashion.
claims.source: Approximately 3 days after being transferred to a new nutrient lawn, the NYL2629 strain began to form tight swarms that tiled most of the petri dish in a semi-periodic fashion (Figure 3B), as has been observed in other strains (de Bono and Bargmann, 1998).
claims.evidence: This is an observation of swarming behavior in the NYL2629 strain, shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The unc-3 mutant C. elegans exhibited large wavefronts of worm aggregates (2–3 cm wide).
claims.source: Based on the hypothesis that this could be driven by partial loss of function in the reporter strain, we then tested for such effects more directly in an unc-3 mutant, where we observed qualitatively different swarming behavior: large wavefronts of worm aggregates (2–3 cm wide) (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is an observation of swarming behavior in the unc-3 mutant, shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Aggregative behavior was not observed in the wildtype C. elegans line.
claims.source: Notably, such aggregative behavior was not observed in the wildtype line (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a negative observation in the wildtype line, shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Recent research on collective behavior has demonstrated that swarming behaviors are modulated by various factors, including oxygen levels and animal density.
claims.source: Recent research on collective behavior has demonstrated that swarming behaviors are modulated by various factors, including oxygen levels and animal density (Demir et al., 2020; Ding et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on C. elegans swarming behavior.

claims.claim: The MCAM is a useful tool for the quantitative study of factors that control social clustering and swarming in C. elegans.
claims.source: While further investigation of the underlying causes and spatiotemporal features of swarming in these different strains is needed, our data clearly demonstrate that the MCAM is a useful tool for the quantitative study of factors that control social clustering and swarming in C. elegans (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the C. elegans experiments, with data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Physarum polycephalum pseudopodia will envelope nutrients in its environment, foraging over a search path spanning many hundreds of square centimeters.
claims.source: For instance, its pseudopodia will envelope nutrients in its environment, foraging over a search path spanning many hundreds of square centimeters (Gawlitta et al., 1980; Rodiek and Hauser, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on slime mold behavior.

claims.claim: The MCAM observed the well-known ability of the slime-mold to traverse mazes, though on much larger spatial scales.
claims.source: Exploiting this, we observed the well-known ability of the slime-mold to traverse mazes, though on much larger spatial scales (Figure 4A; Video 7; Nakagaki et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is an observation of slime mold behavior using the MCAM, shown in Figure 4A and Video 7, with citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Using time-lapse imaging with a 24-camera MCAM array, data was acquired over a 46-hr period, showing the cumulative growth and exploration of a standard 10 cm diameter petri dish that had been seeded with oatmeal flakes.
claims.source: Also, using time-lapse imaging with a 24-camera MCAM array (0.24 gigapixels), we acquired data over a 46-hr period, showing the cumulative growth and exploration of a standard 10 cm diameter petri dish that hadbeen seeded with oatmeal flakes (Video 8).
claims.evidence: This describes a time-lapse experiment with slime mold, shown in Video 8.

claims.claim: By switching to single-camera acquisition mode to acquire at a higher frame rate, the well-known cytoplasmic flow within individual plasmodia was observed.
claims.source: Further, by switching to single-camera acquisition mode to acquire at a higher frame rate, we observed the well-known cytoplasmic flow within individual plasmodia (Durham and Ridgway, 1976), involving particulate matter of tens of square microns, flowing across multiple centimeters (Video 9).
claims.evidence: This is an observation of cytoplasmic flow in slime mold, shown in Video 9, with citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Carpenter ants are nocturnal animals, and their activity levels are very tightly locked to ambient light.
claims.source: Carpenter ants are nocturnal animals, and their activity levels are very tightly locked to ambient light (Narendra et al., 2017; Sharma et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on Carpenter ant behavior.

claims.claim: When light and dark cycles were alternated with small groups of ants, clear fluctuations in activity levels with light cycles were observed, including the dissolution of tight clusters of 'sleeping ants' with increased movement.
claims.source: When we alternated light and dark cycles with small groups of ants, we observed clear fluctuations in activity levels with light cycles, including the dissolution of tight clusters of 'sleeping ants' with increased movement (Figure 4B), but also social interactions and grooming (pulling on antennae with legs; Video 10).
claims.evidence: This is an observation of Carpenter ant behavior using the MCAM, shown in Figure 4B and Video 10.

claims.claim: The MCAM allowed observation of large-scale social behavioral patterns in adult fruit flies, such as face-to-face interactions, and mutations in the wings such as curling.
claims.source: The MCAM allowed us to observe large-scale social behavioral patterns in adult fruit flies, such as face-to-face interactions, and mutations in the wings such as curling (Figure 4C, Video 11).
claims.evidence: This is an observation of Drosophila behavior using the MCAM, shown in Figure 4C and Video 11.

claims.claim: Small features of individual flies could be seen, such as hairs on individual legs, grooming behavior, and the sex of each animal.
claims.source: At the same time, we could see small features of individual flies, such as hairs on individual legs, grooming behavior, and the sex of each animal (Figure 4C, inset).
claims.evidence: This demonstrates the resolution capabilities of the MCAM for Drosophila imaging, shown in Figure 4C inset.

claims.claim: The MCAM technology enables a new suite of imaging experiments for fluorescent specimens, such as tracking freely moving organisms that emit fluorescence via neuronal genetically encoded calcium indicators.
claims.source: Finally, the MCAM technology also enables a new suite of imaging experiments for fluorescent specimens, such as tracking freely moving organisms that emit fluorescence via neuronal genetically encoded calcium indicators, such as GCaMP6 (Dana et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the MCAM's fluorescence imaging capabilities, with citation to GCaMP6.

claims.claim: After outfitting the MCAM imaging system for epi-fluorescence imaging, wide-field fluorescence video of multiple freely moving Drosophila larvae and freely swimming zebrafish was captured.
claims.source: After outfitting the MCAM imaging system for epi-fluorescence imaging, we captured wide-field fluorescence video of multiple freely moving Drosophila larvae and freely swimming zebrafish.
claims.evidence: This describes fluorescence imaging experiments performed with the MCAM.

claims.claim: The MCAM's overlapping fields-of-view were utilized to jointly capture two fluorescence spectral channels simultaneously (i.e. both red and green fluorescence emission) within its recorded videos.
claims.source: We also utilized the MCAM's overlapping fields-of-view to jointly capture two fluorescence spectral channels simultaneously (i.e. both red and green fluorescence emission) within its recorded videos, which may be applied to ratiometric fluorescent image analysis in future studies.
claims.evidence: This describes a dual-channel fluorescence imaging capability of the MCAM.

claims.claim: The MCAM's parallelized imaging design overcomes the limitations of single-objective and single-sensor systems, allowing the acquisition of high-resolution images over a large, in principle infinite FOV.
claims.source: Our parallelized imaging design overcomes the limitations of single-objective and single-sensor systems, allowing the acquisition of high-resolution images over a large, in principle infinite FOV.
claims.evidence: This is a summary claim about the advantages of the MCAM's design.

claims.claim: Prior designs have considered multiple microscopes to image distinct regions in parallel, or via cascaded multiscale lens designs that can yield light-field-type imaging measurements.
claims.source: While prior designs have considered multiple microscopes to image distinct regions in parallel (Weinstein et al., 2004), or via cascaded multiscale lens designs (Fan et al., 2019) that can yield light-field-type imaging measurements (Broxton et al., 2013; Levoy et al., 2009), the MCAM provides a novel, flexible arrangement that can monitor phenomena in freely moving organisms at multiple spatial scales.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on multi-microscope and multiscale lens designs.

claims.claim: The MCAM provides a novel, flexible arrangement that can monitor phenomena in freely moving organisms at multiple spatial scales.
claims.source: While prior designs have considered multiple microscopes to image distinct regions in parallel (Weinstein et al., 2004), or via cascaded multiscale lens designs (Fan et al., 2019) that can yield light-field-type imaging measurements (Broxton et al., 2013; Levoy et al., 2009), the MCAM provides a novel, flexible arrangement that can monitor phenomena in freely moving organisms at multiple spatial scales.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and advantages of the MCAM compared to prior work.

claims.claim: The number of cameras can be varied to produce different FOVs with varying frame rates, depending on the targeted imaging application.
claims.source: The number of cameras can be varied to produce different FOVs with varying frame rates, depending on the targeted imaging application.
claims.evidence: This describes the flexibility of the MCAM design.

claims.claim: The working distance can be changed to jointly increase or decrease the degree of inter-camera FOV overlap to unlock novel functionality.
claims.source: The working distance can also be changed to jointly increase or decrease the degree of inter-camera FOV overlap to unlock novel functionality.
claims.evidence: This describes another aspect of the MCAM's design flexibility.

claims.claim: By adopting a parallelized approach to video acquisition, the MCAM removes a longstanding bottleneck of current single-camera microscope designs to provide researchers with greater flexibility.
claims.source: By adopting a parallelized approach to video acquisition, the MCAM removes a longstanding bottleneck of current single-camera microscope designs to provide researchers with greater flexibility, in particular for observing model organisms at high-resolution in an unconstrained manner.
claims.evidence: This is a summary claim about the advantages of the MCAM's parallelized design.

claims.claim: The MCAM demonstrated two unique capabilities: 3D tracking and simultaneous acquisition of fluorescence images from two unique spectral bands.
claims.source: We have also demonstrated two unique capabilities of the MCAM's multi-lens architecture – 3D tracking and simultaneous acquisition of fluorescence images from two unique spectral bands (see example in Appendix 1—figure 8).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of two novel capabilities demonstrated with the MCAM, with example in Appendix 1—figure 8.

claims.claim: 3D tracking opens up a new dimension to behavioral analysis.
claims.source: The former functionality opens up a new dimension to behavioral analysis, while the latter could lead to novel fluorescence imaging experiments with additional development and refinement.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the potential impact of the MCAM's 3D tracking capability.

claims.claim: Dual-channel fluorescence imaging could lead to novel fluorescence imaging experiments with additional development and refinement.
claims.source: The former functionality opens up a new dimension to behavioral analysis, while the latter could lead to novel fluorescence imaging experiments with additional development and refinement.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential of the MCAM's dual-channel fluorescence capability.

claims.claim: There are likely a wide variety of alternative exciting functionalities that MCAM overlapped sampling can facilitate, such as dense height map estimation at high resolution over large areas via photogrammetric methods.
claims.source: There are likely a wide variety of alternative exciting functionalities that MCAM overlapped sampling can facilitate, such as dense height map estimation at high resolution over large areas via photogrammetric methods (Zhou et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential future applications of the MCAM, with citation to photogrammetric methods.

claims.claim: The MCAM was only able to sample gigapixel images at 1 Hz for up to 60 min.
claims.source: First, while we were only able to sample gigapixel images at 1 Hz for up to 60 min – a significant increase in speed and duration from previous published efforts (Brady et al., 2012) – many biological applications could benefit from much faster acquisition rates.
claims.evidence: This is a stated limitation of the current MCAM system, with comparison to prior work.

claims.claim: The current acquisition speed of 1 Hz is too slow to determine specific patterns in swim kinematics in freely swimming zebrafish.
claims.source: For instance, our current acquisition speed of 1 Hz is too slow to determine specific patterns in swim kinematics in freely swimming zebrafish (Marques et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a stated limitation of the current MCAM system for certain applications, with citation.

claims.claim: A number of strategies are available to increase MCAM sampling rates, including utilizing an updated version of USB that allows approximately 10X faster data transfer.
claims.source: The most straightforward paths to directly increasing the MCAM frame rate are (1) utilizing an updated version of USB that now allows approximately 10 X faster data transfer, (2) distributing data transmission across multiple desktop computers, (3) adopting an alternative FPGA data transfer scheme (e.g. replacing USB data transmission with a faster PCIe protocol), and (4) executing on-chip pixel binning, image cropping, and/or lossless compression to increase temporal sampling rates at the expense of spatial sampling.
claims.evidence: This describes potential future improvements to the MCAM system.

claims.claim: Various combinations of strategies to increase frame rate are currently being explored to facilitate true video-rate (24–30 Hz) MCAM imaging and to achieve significantly higher frame rates and improve cross-camera snapshot synchronization.
claims.source: Various combinations of the above strategies are currently being explored to facilitate true video-rate (24–30 Hz) MCAM imaging and to achieve significantly higher frame rates and improve cross-camera snapshot synchronization.
claims.evidence: This describes ongoing development efforts to improve the MCAM system.

claims.claim: A promising direction is to dynamically pre-process acquired images on the included FPGAs before directing them to computer memory to lighten data transfer loads.
claims.source: A third promising direction is to dynamically pre-process acquired images on the included FPGAs before directing them to computer memory to lighten data transfer loads.
claims.evidence: This describes a potential future improvement to the MCAM system.

claims.claim: CMOS sensors with increased sensitivity and a higher imaging NA could increase fluorescence signal-to-noise ratio and potentially facilitate fluorescence detection at the cellular scale.
claims.source: Second, while we have demonstrated the MCAM's fundamental ability to acquire wide-field fluorescence video of dynamic organism movement (see Supplement), CMOS sensors with increased sensitivity and a higher imaging NA could increase fluorescence signal-to-noise ratio and potentially facilitate fluorescence detect at the cellular scale.
claims.evidence: This describes a potential future improvement to the MCAM's fluorescence imaging capabilities.

claims.claim: Improvements in ratiometric acquisition and the potential addition of optical sectioning could increase fluorescence signal fidelity, most notably during rapid organism movement.
claims.source: Improvements in ratiometric acquisition and the potential addition of optical sectioning could also increase fluorescence signal fidelity, most notably during rapid organism movement.
claims.evidence: This describes potential future improvements to the MCAM's fluorescence imaging capabilities.

claims.claim: With appropriate effort, the MCAM architecture could soon unlock high-quality measurement of functional fluorescence activity during free organism movement over truly macroscopic areas.
claims.source: With appropriate effort, the MCAM architecture could soon unlock high-quality measurement of functional fluorescence activity during free organism movement over truly macroscopic areas, thus yielding a new imaging platform for neuroscientific experiment.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about the future potential of the MCAM for neuroscience applications.

claims.claim: The demonstrated lateral resolution of 18 µm full-pitch is typically not sufficient to resolve individual cells unless they are sparsely labeled.
claims.source: Finally, while the demonstrated lateral resolution in this work (18 µm full-pitch) is typically not sufficient to resolve individual cells unless they are sparsely labeled, tighter camera packing and updated imaging optics may unlock the ability to observe cellular-scale detail in future designs.
claims.evidence: This is a stated limitation of the current MCAM system's resolution.

claims.claim: Tighter camera packing and updated imaging optics may unlock the ability to observe cellular-scale detail in future MCAM designs.
claims.source: Finally, while the demonstrated lateral resolution in this work (18 µm full-pitch) is typically not sufficient to resolve individual cells unless they are sparsely labeled, tighter camera packing and updated imaging optics may unlock the ability to observe cellular-scale detail in future designs.
claims.evidence: This describes a potential future improvement to the MCAM's resolution capabilities.

claims.claim: Large area, high-resolution imaging is important in industrial inspection of manufactured goods and materials, as well as semiconductor metrology.
claims.source: Large area, high-resolution imaging is important in industrial inspection of manufactured goods (Yang et al., 2020) and materials (Ngan et al., 2011), as well as semiconductor metrology (Huang and Pan, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published research on industrial imaging applications.

claims.claim: Large area, high-resolution imaging methods are required for defect detection on semiconductor wafer surfaces.
claims.source: For instance, such methods are required for defect detection on semiconductor wafer surfaces.
claims.evidence: This is an example of an industrial application for large area, high-resolution imaging.

claims.claim: Large area, high-resolution imaging can unlock new functionalities in imaging large pathology specimens, such as whole-mount brain slices.
claims.source: It can also unlock new functionalities in imaging large pathology specimens, such as whole-mount brain slices (Axer et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on pathology imaging, suggesting a potential application for the MCAM.

claims.claim: Biological researchers may be able to utilize the MCAM platform to monitor bacterial colonies and cell cultures over macroscopically large areas.
claims.source: Biological researchers may also be able to utilize the MCAM platform to monitor bacterial colonies (Shi et al., 2017) and cell cultures over macroscopically large areas.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential biological applications of the MCAM, with citation.

claims.claim: The MCAM architecture fits within a growing body of computational imaging hardware that is specifically designed not for direct human viewing, but with the assumption that data post-processing will be used to extract relevant information.
claims.source: In summary, our MCAM architecture fits within a growing body of computational imaging hardware (Mait et al., 2018) that is specifically designed not for direct human viewing, but instead with the assumption that data post-processing will be used to extract relevant information for subsequent analysis.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published research on computational imaging, placing the MCAM in context.

claims.claim: Simultaneously improving processing software (e.g. 3D organism tracking, machine learning-assisted analysis) will prove critical to fully realize the MCAM's benefits.
claims.source: While novel display technology currently enables visual assessment of the MCAM's gigapixel videos that can be many Terabytes in raw size, we anticipate that simultaneously improving processing software (e.g. 3D organism tracking, machine learning-assisted analysis) will prove critical to fully realize the microscope's benefits.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the importance of software development for the MCAM.

claims.claim: As image sensor technology continues to improve with automated processing moving on-chip, the parallelized imaging architecture can help overcome the standard tradeoff between resolution and field-of-view while yielding manageable information-rich datasets.
claims.source: As image sensor technology continues to improve with such automated processing moving on-chip (Amir et al., 2018; Posch et al., 2014), we anticipate that our parallelized imaging architecture can help overcome the standard tradeoff between resolution and field-of-view while at the same time yield manageable information-rich datasets to provide new insight into complex biological systems.
claims.evidence: This is a forward-looking claim about the future potential of the MCAM architecture, with citations to on-chip processing technology.

claims.claim: A Faster-RCNN object detection network was adapted to automate the detection of zebrafish in stitched MCAM images.
claims.source: We adapted a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based object detection algorithm (Faster-RCNN) to automate the detection of zebrafish in stitched MCAM images (Figure 2A), which are too large for training or inference on existing graphical processing units (GPUs).
claims.evidence: This describes the use of a CNN for object detection in MCAM images, shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: MCAM images are too large for training or inference on existing graphical processing units (GPUs).
claims.source: We adapted a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based object detection algorithm (Faster-RCNN) to automate the detection of zebrafish in stitched MCAM images (Figure 2A), which are too large for training or inference on existing graphical processing units (GPUs).
claims.evidence: This is a stated technical challenge of working with gigapixel MCAM images.

claims.claim: Transfer learning with a data augmentation pipeline that included supplementing training data with synthetically generated occluder fish yielded a network that could accurately detect individual zebrafish even when they occluded one another.
claims.source: We used transfer learning with a data augmentation pipeline that included supplementing training data with synthetically generated occluder fish (similar to that described in István et al., 2018; Sárándi et al., 2018), because occlusion was relatively rare in the original data. After training, this yielded a network that could accurately detect individual zebrafish even when they occluded one another (Appendix 1—figure 5I, Video 3).
claims.evidence: This describes the training approach and results for the zebrafish detection network, with results shown in Appendix 1—figure 5I and Video 3.

claims.claim: The high spatial resolution of the MCAM was exploited to consistently recognize individual zebrafish by morphological differences.
claims.source: To track individual zebrafish over time, we exploited the high spatial resolution of the MCAM to consistently recognize individuals by morphological differences (Figure 2B), which has not been shown before in zebrafish younger than 21 days old.
claims.evidence: This describes a novel capability enabled by the MCAM's resolution, shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Consistent recognition of individual zebrafish by morphological differences has not been shown before in zebrafish younger than 21 days old.
claims.source: To track individual zebrafish over time, we exploited the high spatial resolution of the MCAM to consistently recognize individuals by morphological differences (Figure 2B), which has not been shown before in zebrafish younger than 21 days old.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the zebrafish identification capability.

claims.claim: A Siamese neural network was trained that was able to learn to track the same zebrafish across multiple frames.
claims.source: Specifically, we trained a Siamese neural network (Bertinetto et al., 2021; Appendix 1—figure 6) that was able to learn to track the same zebrafish across multiple frames (Figure 2C).

results.result: Current imaging systems face fundamental tradeoffs between field of view and resolution, preventing simultaneous observation of biological processes across multiple spatial scales. Complex biological systems span many orders of magnitude in spatial scale, but no single imaging system currently allows unrestricted access to all scales simultaneously.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C10 establish the scientific motivation and gap in existing technology. These are well-supported by citations to established literature (C7, C8) and represent accepted knowledge about imaging system limitations (C9, C10). The claims accurately describe the problem the MCAM addresses.

results.result: Existing approaches to imaging freely moving organisms have significant limitations. Head-fixation restricts natural behavior, while tracking microscopes are limited to single organisms and cannot scale to observe multiple organisms simultaneously at high resolution over large areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C16 are well-supported by multiple citations to published research. The limitations of head-fixation (C11-C12) and tracking microscopes (C13-C16) are documented in the cited literature. These claims accurately characterize the state of the field and establish context for the MCAM's advantages.

results.result: Alternative imaging strategies including time-sequential scanning and reducing magnification have fundamental limitations. Time-sequential approaches cannot simultaneously observe living processes, while reducing magnification trades off spatial resolution and can miss morphological features and behavioral signatures.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C22 are supported by citations to published research and describe well-known limitations of existing approaches. The reasoning about why these approaches are inadequate for the target application is sound and logically consistent.

results.result: Single-lens imaging systems face fundamental optical and practical limitations. Geometrical aberrations increase nonlinearly with lens diameter, requiring additional corrective lenses that increase cost and complexity. Most commercial microscope lenses transfer less than 50 megapixels, and even specialized gigapixel systems are prohibitively expensive.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C29 are well-supported by citations to optical physics literature and technical specifications. The claim about the $168 million telescope camera (C29) provides concrete evidence of cost barriers. The logical progression from optical principles to practical limitations is sound.

results.result: The MCAM is a scalable multi-camera array microscope that enables gigapixel-scale imaging with 18 μm resolution over hundreds of square centimeters. The system uses up to 96 cameras with overlapping fields of view, costs significantly less than alternatives, and can theoretically scale to arbitrarily large fields of view.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C4, C30-C37 describe the core MCAM system and its capabilities. These are supported by technical specifications, cost data (C31, C54-C57), and demonstrations with multiple species (C5, C36). The claim of linear cost scaling (C30) is supported by the modular architecture. The theoretical scalability claim (C35) is appropriately qualified as theoretical.

results.result: The MCAM hardware consists of 96 CMOS sensors (10 MP each, 1.4 μm pixels) arranged in an 8×12 array with 19 mm pitch, using 25 mm focal length lenses. The system operates at 1 Hz in full-frame mode or 12 Hz in single-sensor mode, achieving 18 μm full-pitch resolution at 150 mm working distance.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C48 provide detailed technical specifications that are internally consistent and supported by the Methods section. The specifications are precise and verifiable. The frame rate limitations (C43, C46) are clearly stated. Resolution measurements (C48) are supported by Appendix 1—figure 2.

results.result: The MCAM's depth of field is characterized by three measures: theoretical Rayleigh criterion of 0.28 mm, experimental axial range of 2.54 mm where resolution remains within 2× of maximum, and contrast FWHM of 1.95 mm.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 provide complementary measures of depth of field. C49 is a theoretical calculation, while C50-C51 are experimental measurements. The use of multiple metrics is appropriate for characterizing depth of field. The experimental measurements are stated to be in Appendix 1.

results.result: The MCAM design uses rectangular sensors to achieve 52% overlap along the longer dimension and <10% along the shorter dimension, ensuring any point is imaged by at least two cameras. The total component cost for 96 cameras is $14,352 ($30 per sensor, $75 per lens, $267 per FPGA).
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53 describe the overlapping configuration that enables stitching and stereoscopic imaging. Claims C54-C57 provide detailed cost breakdown that supports the affordability claims. The arithmetic in C57 is verifiable: (96×$30) + (96×$75) + (16×$267) = $14,352.

results.result: The MCAM recorded continuously at 0.74 Hz for one hour, generating 2.5 TB of raw data and 1.17 TB of stitched data. The system achieves approximately 1 GB/s write speed using solid state drives, representing a significant speedup over previous gigapixel systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 provide concrete performance data from actual experiments. The data volumes are consistent with the stated specifications (96 cameras × 10 MP × ~1 Hz). The comparison to prior work (C59) is supported by citation to Brady et al., 2012.

results.result: In MCAM images, 8 dpf zebrafish are captured by 9699±2758 pixels (n=93), compared to less than 400 pixels with a 20 MP camera or ~100 pixels with a 3 MP camera covering the same field of view.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 provides quantitative data with sample size and standard deviation. Claims C61-C62 provide comparative calculations that demonstrate the MCAM's advantage. The comparisons are fair (same FOV) and the calculations are reasonable. Figure 1E provides visual confirmation of C62.

results.result: A Faster-RCNN object detection network was adapted for gigapixel-scale zebrafish detection. Because MCAM images are too large for standard GPU processing, the network was trained on image patches. Transfer learning with synthetic occlusion augmentation enabled accurate detection even when zebrafish occluded one another.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C111 describe the object detection approach with appropriate technical detail. The challenge of GPU memory limitations (C110) is a known issue with gigapixel images. The use of synthetic occlusion (C111) is supported by citations and results shown in Appendix 1—figure 5I and Video 3. The approach is methodologically sound.

results.result: The MCAM's high resolution enabled individual identification of zebrafish younger than 21 days old by morphological differences, which has not been shown before. A Siamese neural network was trained to track individual fish across frames using melanophore patterns and body morphology. The resolution also enabled tail tracking and eye position measurement.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C116 describe novel capabilities enabled by the MCAM's resolution. The novelty claim (C113) is appropriately qualified. The Siamese network approach (C114) is supported by Figure 2C showing clear clustering by individual identity. The behavioral measurements (C116) are demonstrated in Figures 2D-E. This represents a significant technical achievement.

results.result: The MCAM's overlapping field-of-view configuration enables stereoscopic depth tracking with approximately 100 μm accuracy over a >5 mm depth range. The system uses scale-invariant feature transforms to match features between adjacent cameras and calculate depth from disparity, revealing 3D swim trajectories typically inaccessible without dual-view systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C63, C117-C121 describe the stereoscopic depth tracking capability. The accuracy specification (C63) is supported by experimental validation in Appendix 1—figure 7. The algorithm description (C120) is technically sound. Figure 2F-G demonstrates the capability with zebrafish 3D trajectories. This is a novel capability enabled by the MCAM architecture.

results.result: The MCAM successfully imaged multiple model organisms including C. elegans at high resolution over large areas. Videos captured approximately 58,000 worms per frame at 450 pixels per worm. Previously unreported swarming behavior was observed in NYL2629 and unc-3 mutant strains but not in wildtype, demonstrating the MCAM's utility for studying collective behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C64-C68, C122-C124 demonstrate the MCAM's versatility across species. The quantitative data (C64) is substantial. The novel observations of swarming behavior (C65-C67) are clearly documented in Figure 3 and Videos 4-6. The negative control (C68) strengthens the findings. CNN-based segmentation (C123) and computer vision tracking (C124) demonstrate appropriate analysis methods.

results.result: Quantitative analysis of C. elegans revealed significant differences in worm and swarm density across strains. Wildtype had 154±0.254 worms/cm² and 1.85±0.01 swarms/cm², NYL2629 had 262±1.126 worms/cm² and 45.92±0.073 swarms/cm², and Unc3 had 36±0.203 worms/cm² and 10.65±0.025 swarms/cm². Despite higher worm density, wildtype formed significantly fewer swarms than Unc3 (p=2.3×10⁻⁶⁶, Cohen's d=0.96).
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C131 provide detailed quantitative data with appropriate statistics. The measurements are precise with small error bars. The statistical comparison (C131) uses appropriate tests (one-sided t-test) and reports both p-value and effect size. The large effect size and extremely small p-value indicate a robust finding. Figure 3E visualizes these data.

results.result: The MCAM is a useful tool for quantitative study of factors controlling social clustering and swarming in C. elegans. Recent research shows swarming behaviors are modulated by oxygen levels and animal density, and further investigation of the underlying causes is needed.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 appropriately contextualize the findings with citations to recent literature and acknowledge that further investigation is needed. The claim that MCAM is useful for this research (C70) is supported by the demonstrated capabilities and quantitative data in Figure 3E.

results.result: The MCAM successfully imaged slime mold (Physarum polycephalum) behavior across multiple spatial and temporal scales, including maze traversal over 96 hours, growth and exploration over 46 hours in a petri dish, and cytoplasmic flow at higher frame rates in single-camera mode.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74 demonstrate the MCAM's capability for time-lapse imaging and multi-scale observation. The maze traversal (C72) is shown in Figure 4A and Video 7. The 46-hour time-lapse (C73) is in Video 8. The cytoplasmic flow observation (C74) demonstrates the flexibility of single-camera mode. All observations are supported by appropriate citations to prior work on slime mold behavior.

results.result: Carpenter ant activity levels are tightly locked to ambient light. When light and dark cycles were alternated, clear fluctuations in activity were observed, including dissolution of sleeping ant clusters and increased movement, as well as social interactions and grooming.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 demonstrate the MCAM's capability for behavioral observation in social insects. The light-locked behavior (C75) is supported by citations. The observations (C76) are documented in Figure 4B and Video 10. The ability to resolve fine details like grooming demonstrates the system's resolution.

results.result: The MCAM enabled observation of large-scale social behavioral patterns in adult Drosophila, including face-to-face interactions and wing mutations, while simultaneously resolving small features such as hairs on individual legs, grooming behavior, and sex determination.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 demonstrate the MCAM's multi-scale imaging capability with Drosophila. The observations are documented in Figure 4C and Video 11. The ability to simultaneously observe population-level behavior and individual-level morphology represents a key advantage of the MCAM approach.

results.result: The MCAM enables fluorescence imaging of freely moving organisms, including dual-channel fluorescence acquisition using overlapping fields of view. Wide-field fluorescence video was captured of freely moving Drosophila larvae and zebrafish expressing genetically encoded calcium indicators.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81, C88 describe the MCAM's fluorescence imaging capabilities. The demonstrations with GCaMP6-expressing organisms (C79-C80) show proof-of-concept. The dual-channel capability (C81) is a novel feature enabled by the overlapping FOV design. However, the authors appropriately note this requires further development (see C90, C97-C99).

results.result: The MCAM's parallelized imaging design overcomes limitations of single-objective systems, allowing high-resolution imaging over large fields of view. The system provides a novel, flexible arrangement compared to prior multi-microscope or multiscale lens designs, with adjustable camera number, frame rate, and working distance.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C87 summarize the MCAM's advantages and novelty. The comparison to prior work (C83) is supported by appropriate citations. The flexibility claims (C85-C86) are supported by the demonstrated operational modes. The overall assessment (C87) is justified by the demonstrated capabilities across multiple species and applications.

results.result: The MCAM's unique capabilities open new research directions. 3D tracking adds a new dimension to behavioral analysis, dual-channel fluorescence could enable novel experiments with further development, and overlapped sampling could facilitate applications like dense height map estimation via photogrammetric methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C91 are largely speculative about future applications. While C89 is supported by the demonstrated 3D tracking capability, C90 explicitly requires 'additional development and refinement,' and C91 is purely speculative ('likely a wide variety'). These are reasonable projections but not demonstrated results.

results.result: The current MCAM is limited to 1 Hz frame rate for gigapixel imaging, which is too slow for some applications like zebrafish swim kinematics. Multiple strategies are available or being explored to increase frame rates, including faster USB, distributed computing, alternative FPGA protocols, on-chip processing, and pixel binning.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C96 honestly acknowledge current limitations and propose solutions. The 1 Hz limitation (C92) is clearly stated with comparison to prior work. The specific limitation for zebrafish kinematics (C93) is supported by citation. The proposed solutions (C94-C96) are technically reasonable, though C95-C96 are speculative about future work.

results.result: The MCAM's fluorescence imaging capabilities could be improved with higher sensitivity sensors, higher NA optics, improved ratiometric acquisition, and optical sectioning. With appropriate effort, the system could enable high-quality functional fluorescence imaging during free movement over macroscopic areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99 are speculative about future improvements to fluorescence imaging. While the proposed improvements (C97-C98) are technically reasonable, they have not been demonstrated. The claim that the system 'could soon unlock' these capabilities (C99) is optimistic but not supported by current data.

results.result: The demonstrated 18 μm resolution is typically insufficient to resolve individual cells unless sparsely labeled. Tighter camera packing and updated optics may enable cellular-scale detail in future designs.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 honestly acknowledge resolution limitations. The assessment that 18 μm is insufficient for most cellular imaging (C100) is accurate. The suggestion for future improvement (C101) is reasonable but speculative. This represents appropriate acknowledgment of current limitations.

results.result: Large-area, high-resolution imaging has applications beyond model organism research, including industrial inspection, semiconductor metrology, pathology, and monitoring bacterial colonies and cell cultures. The MCAM platform could potentially be utilized for these applications.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C105 discuss potential applications beyond the demonstrated uses. The importance of large-area imaging in these fields (C102-C103) is supported by citations. The potential applications to pathology and cell culture (C104-C105) are appropriately qualified as speculative ('can unlock,' 'may be able to').

results.result: The MCAM fits within computational imaging approaches designed for post-processing rather than direct viewing. Improving processing software will be critical to realize the system's benefits. As sensor technology improves with on-chip processing, the parallelized architecture can overcome resolution/FOV tradeoffs while yielding manageable datasets.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 appropriately contextualize the MCAM within computational imaging (C106, supported by citation). The emphasis on software development (C107) is justified given the massive data volumes. The forward-looking statement (C108) is appropriately qualified as anticipatory and supported by citations to on-chip processing technology.
